monstera.name: Monstera (Swiss cheese plant)

care.water: Every 7–10 days, once the top 2 cm of soil is dry
care.light: Bright indirect light, avoid direct sun

monstera.description: The queen of houseplants! The characteristic holes in its leaves (fenestration) help it withstand tropical storms and let more light through to the lower layers.
funFacts: In the wild it climbs trees up to 20 m high
The fruit, once ripe (it takes a year!), tastes like a mix of banana and pineapple
Leaf holes (fenestration) only appear after 2–3 years
Aerial roots can be guided into the soil – they take up water and nutrients
The name “deliciosa” comes from its edible fruit
In rainforests it grows in the shade, climbing towards the light
diseases: Yellow leaves = overwatering or a lack of minerals
Brown spots = sunburn or calcium deficiency
Black spots = fungus from too much water – water less
No holes in the leaves = too little light or the plant is too young
Curling leaves = too dry or too cold
monstera.propagation: Stem cuttings with at least 1 node and an aerial root. Root in water or perlite – roots appear after 2–4 weeks.

pothos.name: Pothos (Devil's ivy)

care.water: Every 7–14 days, very tolerant of drying out
care.light: From deep shade to bright – exceptionally tolerant

pothos.description: Practically indestructible! It grows even in dark offices and tolerates weeks without water. It filters formaldehyde and benzene from the air.
funFacts: NASA placed pothos in its TOP 10 air-purifying plants
In the wild its leaves grow up to 1 metre wide!
It can grow in plain water for many years
It rarely flowers indoors – in the wild it flowers after 10+ years
It absorbs carbon monoxide – a natural air detox
There are 15+ coloured varieties: Golden, Marble Queen, Neon, Manjula…
diseases: Yellow leaves = overwatering (the most common mistake!)
Pale or all-green leaves on a variegated form = too little light
Brown tips = dry air or salts in the water – use boiled water
Rotting stem = cold + excess moisture
pothos.propagation: The easiest plant to propagate! Cut a stem with 2–3 nodes and put it in water. Roots appear after 1–2 weeks.

sansevieria.name: Snake plant (Sansevieria)

care.water: Every 2–4 weeks, in winter once every 2 months
care.light: From deep shade to full sun

sansevieria.description: An indestructible icon! The only popular plant that produces oxygen AT NIGHT (CAM photosynthesis). Ideal for the bedroom. Survives months of neglect.
funFacts: The only popular houseplant that releases oxygen at night (CAM cycle)
In Africa its leaf fibres were used to make bowstrings, ropes and fabric
It can survive 2–3 months completely without water
NASA recommends it as an air filter for space stations
The Moonshine variety has almost silver leaves – a rare look
It can grow in one pot for decades without repotting
diseases: Soft, rotting leaves = overwatering – the main killer! Water less
Wrinkled leaves = it needs water (rare)
Brown tips = sunburn or cold
Pale stripes fading = too little light on variegated forms
sansevieria.propagation: Division (fastest) or leaf cuttings: cut a leaf into 5 cm pieces, let them dry for 2 days and plant in sand. Roots appear after 1–2 months.

ficus-lyrata.name: Fiddle-leaf fig

care.water: Every 7–10 days, once the top 2–3 cm is dry
care.light: Bright indirect, AVOID harsh sun and draughts

ficus-lyrata.description: The star of Instagram and interior magazines! Huge violin-shaped leaves. Very fussy – it dislikes being moved and may drop leaves because of a draught.
funFacts: In the wild it grows to 15 m and strangles other trees (strangler fig)
A single leaf can be 45 cm long and 30 cm wide
After being moved it may drop half its leaves from stress – that is normal
It needs a fixed spot – mark the direction of the light and don't turn the pot
Around 1900 it was a symbol of luxury in European drawing rooms
diseases: Brown spots with a yellow halo = bacterial infection from irregular watering
Dropping leaves = stress (new spot, temperature, draught) – don't panic
Yellow lower leaves = natural ageing or overwatering
Red specks = oedema from too much water
White dots = scale insects or whitefly – wipe with alcohol
ficus-lyrata.propagation: Tip cuttings (15 cm) or air layering. Rooting hormone is essential. Harder than other figs.

spathiphyllum.name: Peace lily

care.water: Every 5–7 days, likes evenly moist soil
care.light: From deep shade to bright indirect

spathiphyllum.description: The peace lily! It droops dramatically when thirsty but bounces back immediately after watering. It can flower all year round. A great air filter.
funFacts: One of NASA's TOP 10 air-purifying plants
The white “flower” is a modified leaf (spathe); the real flowers are tiny
It can flower all year round in good light
One of the best natural filters for ammonia and acetone
Flat drooping is an alarm signal – it recovers within 30 minutes of watering
In the wild it flowers only once a year – indoors it can bloom more often
diseases: Drooping = it needs water – water at once, it recovers in 30 min
Yellow leaves = overwatering or an old leaf (natural)
Brown tips = chlorine/fluoride in the water – use boiled water
No flowers = too little light or too low a temperature
spathiphyllum.propagation: Divide clumps when repotting. Each part must have roots and at least 2–3 leaves. Best done in spring.

philodendron.name: Heartleaf philodendron

care.water: Every 7–10 days, once the top is dry

philodendron.description: A classic climber with charming heart-shaped leaves. It grows fast, propagates easily and is exceptionally forgiving. Very similar to pothos, but with matte leaves.
funFacts: The genus Philodendron has over 450 described species!
The name means “tree lover” – in the wild it climbs trees
The Brasil variety has yellow-green streaks like the Brazilian flag
Aerial roots help it climb and take moisture from the air
New leaves emerge rolled up and brownish-pink – that is normal!
diseases: Yellow leaves = overwatering
Small leaves = too little light or fertiliser
Brown tips = dry air – mist more often
Long bare stretches of stem between leaves = too little light
philodendron.propagation: Very easy! Cuttings with a node in water or soil. Roots appear after 2–3 weeks.

pilea.name: Chinese money plant (Pilea)

care.water: Every 7–10 days, once the top is dry

pilea.description: The friendship plant! It produces lots of “babies” (offsets) you can give to friends. Round leaves on long stalks look like coins.
funFacts: For decades it was passed on only as cuttings – almost impossible to buy
It was only formally described by botanists in 1984!
Also called the “UFO plant” because of its leaf shape
Turn it every week – it quickly leans towards the light
It produces dozens of “babies” a year – the perfect gift
It comes from Yunnan province in China, where it grows in damp forests
diseases: Curling leaves = too much sun or it needs water
Yellow lower leaves = natural ageing or overwatering
Dropping leaves = draught or cold
Pale leaves = too little light
pilea.propagation: It makes babies on its own! Cut off offsets when they are 5–7 cm tall with their own roots. Stems can also be rooted in water.

ficus-elastica.name: Rubber plant
ficus-elastica.description: A small tree with spectacular glossy leaves. Once the main source of natural rubber. The Burgundy variety has almost black leaves – very stylish.
funFacts: In the 19th century it was a major source of rubber – hence the name “rubber plant”
In the wild it grows up to 30 m tall!
In India its roots are trained into living root bridges
The Tineke variety has pink and cream variegation
The milky sap from a cut is strongly irritating – wear gloves
diseases: Dropping leaves = stress (cold, draught, new spot)
Yellow leaves = overwatering
Brown spots = sunburn
Dusty leaves = wipe regularly with a damp cloth (dust blocks photosynthesis)
ficus-elastica.propagation: Tip cuttings or air layering. Milky sap – wear gloves! Rooting hormone speeds things up.

dracaena.name: Dragon tree (Dracaena marginata)

care.water: Every 10–14 days, likes to dry out

dracaena.description: An elegant slender tree with red-edged leaves. Very tolerant of neglect and poor light. Cleans toxins from the air.
funFacts: The name “dracaena” means “female dragon” – its resin is red (dragon's blood)
NASA recommends it for removing formaldehyde indoors
It can live over 100 years – a true heirloom
The Tricolor variety has pink, cream and green stripes
Its stem can form natural spirals and arches – very decorative
diseases: Brown tips = chlorine/fluoride in the water – use rainwater
Yellow lower leaves = natural ageing (1–2 leaves a month is normal)
Soft stem = overwatering and root rot – rescue by repotting
Pale leaves = too little light on coloured varieties
dracaena.propagation: Tip cuttings or stem sections (5–10 cm). They root in water. A cut trunk will sprout new shoots from the side.

zamioculcas.name: ZZ plant (Zamioculcas)

care.water: Every 2–4 weeks or even less often!

zamioculcas.description: ZZ plant – the king of neglect! It survives months without water thanks to its thick rhizomes. Its glossy leaves reflect light like plastic – but they're real!
funFacts: It was only introduced to cultivation in 1996!
It can survive 4–6 months without a single drop of water
It grows even in windowless offices – though very slowly
The Raven variety has almost black leaves – striking on Instagram
Its rhizomes store water like potatoes – the secret of its survival
A single leaf rooted in soil can give a new plant after 6–12 months
diseases: Yellow leaves = OVERWATERING (the main and almost only killer!)
Wrinkled stems = it needs water (rare, but real)
Brown spots = sunburn
No growth in winter = normal dormancy
zamioculcas.propagation: Divide the rhizomes when repotting. Leaf cuttings work, but very slowly (6–12 months). Best divided in spring.

orchid.name: Moth orchid (Phalaenopsis)

care.water: Every 7–10 days by soaking for 15 min

orchid.description: The queen of flowering houseplants! It blooms for 3–6 months. It needs bright but not direct light. The secret to reblooming is cool nights (15°C).
funFacts: It blooms for 3–6 months in a row – one of the longest-flowering plants
Cool nights (15°C) for 2 weeks trigger a new flower spike
In the wild it grows on trees (an epiphyte) – its roots need air
Clear pots are standard – the roots photosynthesise!
The same spike can rebloom 2–3 times if you don't cut it off
There are over 70 Phalaenopsis species and thousands of hybrids
diseases: Yellowing lower leaves = natural (1–2 leaves a year is normal)
Rotting roots (brown, soft) = too much water
Shrivelled, wrinkled leaves = too little water or diseased roots
No flowers = nights too warm – move it to a cooler windowsill
Sticky leaves = mealybugs or aphids – wipe with alcohol
orchid.propagation: Keikis (baby plants on the flower spike) – cut them off once they have their own roots of 3+ cm. Dividing mature plants is also possible.

anthurium.name: Flamingo flower (Anthurium)

care.water: Every 7–10 days, likes evenly moist soil

anthurium.description: The glossy, lacquered “flowers” are actually coloured leaves (spathes). In good conditions it blooms almost non-stop all year round.
funFacts: The red “flower” is a spathe – a modified leaf, not a petal
The real flower is the small spike (spadix) in the middle
It blooms almost non-stop – one of the longest “flowering” plants
Available in red, pink, white, purple, black and green
In the wild it grows as an epiphyte on rainforest trees
diseases: Yellow leaves = overwatering or too much direct light
Brown tips = dry air or fluoride in the water
No flowers = too little light or too low a temperature
Black spots = fungus from excess moisture on the leaves
anthurium.propagation: Division or side offsets. Each part must have roots. Root in sphagnum moss.

kalanchoe.name: Kalanchoe (Flaming Katy)

care.light: Bright, a few hours of direct sun

kalanchoe.description: A popular flowering succulent! Small flowers in red, pink, yellow, orange or white last 4–6 weeks. Very easy to care for.
funFacts: You can force it to rebloom with 6 weeks of darkness (12 h a day)
It comes from Madagascar – an island with a unique flora
Short days (photoperiodism) trigger flower buds
Available in over 100 colours and varieties!
Its leaves store water – it shrugs off weeks of neglect
diseases: Rotting leaves = overwatering – the most common mistake
No flowers = too little light or no dark period
Grey spots on leaves = powdery mildew – improve ventilation
Long, pale shoots = too little sun (etiolation)
kalanchoe.propagation: Leaf or stem cuttings. Let them dry for 2 days and plant in dry sand. Roots appear after 3–4 weeks.

begonia.name: Rex begonia

care.water: Every 7–10 days, keep water off the leaves

begonia.description: The most beautiful begonia! Grown for its spectacular metallic leaves – silver, pink, burgundy and purple with fanciful patterns.
funFacts: Grown mainly for its leaves, not its flowers
The Escargot variety has leaves coiled into a spiral like a snail shell
The metallic sheen comes from special light-reflecting skin cells
There are several thousand (!) begonia varieties and hybrids
It comes from tropical areas where it grows in the shade of rocky cliffs
diseases: Powdery mildew (white fuzz) = poor air circulation + excess moisture
Stem rot = standing water + cold
Brown spots = water on the leaves or sunburn
Dropping leaves = draught or a sudden change in temperature
begonia.propagation: Leaf cuttings – cut a leaf, lay it on damp perlite and press the pieces into the substrate. Roots appear after 4–6 weeks.

african-violet.name: African violet
african-violet.description: A miniature legend! It flowers practically all year round. The key to success is watering from below – water on the leaves leaves spots. Ideal for a windowsill.
funFacts: Discovered in 1892 by Baron von Saint Paul – hence its Latin name
Watering from below (a saucer) is the best method – the leaves dislike water
It blooms almost non-stop all year in the right light
Cold water leaves white spots on the leaves – use lukewarm water
Miniature varieties grow in pots just 5 cm wide! There are 16,000+ varieties
diseases: White spots on leaves = cold water or water poured onto the leaves
Rotting crown = standing water + cold
No flowers = too little light or too large a pot
Greyish-brown leaves = powdery mildew – improve air circulation
african-violet.propagation: Leaf cuttings – cut a healthy leaf with its stalk and put it in water or perlite. Small plantlets appear after 4–6 weeks.

hibiscus.name: Chinese hibiscus

care.water: Every 5–7 days in season, less in winter
care.light: Full sun for at least 4–6 h a day

hibiscus.description: A tropical shrub with huge flowers up to 20 cm across! Each flower lasts only a day, but the plant produces lots of them. The flowers are edible.
funFacts: Each flower lives only 24 hours – but new ones open every day
The flowers are edible – used in teas, salads and liqueurs
A symbol of Malaysia and Hawaii, where it blooms outdoors all year
It needs 4–6 hours of direct sun a day – loves a south-facing window
Reduce water and temperature in winter – the key to spring flowering
diseases: Bud drop = a sudden change of spot or too dry
Yellow leaves = iron or magnesium deficiency, or overwatering
Aphids on new shoots = common – spray with water or soapy water
No flowers = too little sun or too cold
hibiscus.propagation: Semi-ripe cuttings (15 cm) with rooting hormone. Roots appear after 4–6 weeks. It can also be grown from seed.

hoya.name: Wax plant (Hoya)

care.water: Every 10–14 days, a typical trailing succulent
care.light: Bright indirect, a little direct morning sun

hoya.description: The waxy leaves gave this plant the name “wax plant”. Star-shaped flowers gathered in round clusters give off an intense sweet scent – especially at night.
funFacts: The flowers are most fragrant at night – an adaptation to night-time pollinators
Don't cut off the flower stalks after blooming – they will flower again in the same place!
There are 200–500 Hoya species with differently shaped leaves
It likes to be “pot-bound” – too big a pot delays flowering
The Kerrii variety has heart-shaped leaves – a popular symbol of love
diseases: No flowers = too little light or too big a pot
Yellow leaves = overwatering or too few nutrients
Wrinkled leaves = it needs water (rare)
Mealybugs = white fluff in the leaf axils – wipe with alcohol
hoya.propagation: Stem cuttings with 2–3 nodes in water or sphagnum. Roots appear after 3–5 weeks.

begonia-maculata.name: Polka dot begonia

care.water: Every 7 days, once the top 2 cm is dry

begonia-maculata.description: The most Instagrammable plant of recent years! Dark green leaves with silver dots like trout skin, and burgundy undersides. It produces pretty white flowers.
funFacts: Discovered in Brazil in 1820 by the Italian botanist Giuseppe Raddi
The silver dots are a waxy skin finish that reflects excess light
It blooms with small white flowers – a striking contrast with the dark leaves
One of the most fashionable houseplants on social media
It grows fast – it can put on 30 cm in one growing season
diseases: Powdery mildew (white fuzz on leaves) = humid, still air
Dropping leaves = cold or draught
Stem rot = too wet at the base
Brown edges = dry air or fluoride in the water
begonia-maculata.propagation: Stem cuttings of 10–15 cm in water. Very easy – roots appear after 1–2 weeks.

echeveria.name: Echeveria

care.water: Every 14–21 days, let it dry out completely between waterings
care.light: Full sun for 4–6 h a day

echeveria.description: A juicy rosette that looks like a flower! The leaves are covered with a natural waxy bloom (farina) that protects them from the sun. Dozens of colours and shapes.
funFacts: The wax on the leaves (farina) protects against sun and water loss – don't rub it off!
In season it sends up long stalks with small bell-shaped flowers
Water and sun stress bring out red and purple tints in the leaves
There are over 150 species and hundreds of echeveria hybrids
Ideal for succulent arrangements and terrariums
diseases: Stretched, pale shoots = too little sun (etiolation)
Rotting lower leaves = too much water or poor drainage
Wrinkled leaves = it needs water (rare)
Loss of the waxy bloom = damaged skin – don't touch, it grows back
echeveria.propagation: Leaf cuttings (twist off a whole leaf cleanly) or offsets. Lay the leaf on dry sand, don't bury it – the roots will appear on their own.

aloe.name: Aloe vera
aloe.toxic: Yes – the latex under the skin

care.water: Every 2–3 weeks, less often in winter

aloe.description: A first-aid kit in a pot! The gel from its fleshy leaves soothes burns, bites and skin irritation. One of the most widely used medicinal plants in the world.
funFacts: Known for over 3,500 years – mentioned in Egyptian papyri from 1552 BC
Cleopatra reputedly used aloe gel as a daily face cream
The leaf gel contains 200+ biologically active substances
NASA included it among plants that improve air quality
The latex (yellow liquid under the skin) is toxic – only the clear gel is safe
diseases: Brown, soft leaves = overwatering – unpot it and dry the roots
Red or brown leaves = too much sun or cold
Wrinkled leaves = it needs water or the roots are diseased
White spots = sunburn after sudden exposure to the sun
aloe.propagation: Cut off the offsets (pups) once they are 7–10 cm. Let them dry for 2 days and plant in sand or perlite.

crassula.name: Jade plant (Money tree)
crassula.description: A symbol of luck and prosperity in feng shui and Asian cultures. It grows very slowly but lives for decades. It can be shaped into a miniature bonsai.
funFacts: In feng shui it brings wealth – hence the name “money tree”
It can live for decades – even 70–100 years!
After a few years it starts to bloom with small white stars in winter
The trunk turns woody with age and looks like a miniature tree
Cold stress (8–10°C) in autumn triggers exceptional pink flowering
diseases: Soft, drooping leaves = overwatering (the main cause of death!)
Wrinkled leaves = too dry
Brown spots = sunburn after sudden exposure
White crystals on the leaves = natural salt excretion – normal
crassula.propagation: Leaf or stem cuttings. Let them dry for 2–3 days and plant in dry sand. Very easy.

haworthia.name: Zebra plant (Haworthia)

care.light: Bright indirect, tolerates shade (an exception among succulents)

haworthia.description: An exception among succulents – it doesn't need full sun! The white stripes are rows of raised bumps. Ideal for homes with less sunny windows.
funFacts: One of the few succulents that tolerate partial shade
The white bumps on the leaves are tough tissue that reflects excess light
It forms characteristic “clusters” – offset rosettes around the mother plant
In the wild it grows buried in the soil – only the tips show above ground
Prized in Japan as a collector's plant – rare varieties cost a fortune
diseases: Rotting roots = overwatering
Red leaves = too much direct sun
Pale and stretched = too little light
Shrinking = time to water
haworthia.propagation: Cut off offset rosettes with their roots. Let them dry for 2 days and plant.

lithops.name: Living stones (Lithops)

care.water: ONLY in summer and autumn; NO water in winter and spring!
care.light: Full sun for 4–6 h a day

lithops.description: Perfect camouflage! They look like pebbles – an evolutionary trick to avoid plant-eaters. The strangest houseplant in the world.
funFacts: They evolved to look like pebbles – in the wild they are almost invisible among the gravel
Watering in the wrong season = death! No water in winter and spring (while they shed)
Every year they shed – the old leaves split and a new pair emerges
The flowers are bigger than the plant itself and smell lovely
They live for decades if not overwatered
Translucent windows on top let light into the plant
diseases: Splitting or rotting = OVERWATERING in the wrong season (the most common mistake!)
No flowers = too little sun or the wrong watering cycle
Pale colour = too little sun
lithops.propagation: From seed (slow) or by dividing the clump while it sheds.

string-of-pearls.name: String of pearls

care.water: Every 14–21 days, likes to dry out
care.light: Bright with a few hours of sun

string-of-pearls.description: A string of shiny round leaves like beads! Each bead is a reduced leaf that stores water. Stunning trailing from a shelf or hanging basket.
funFacts: The round leaves minimise water loss – an evolutionary marvel
In the wild it trails over rocky cliffs in South Africa and Namibia
It blooms with small white flowers that smell of cinnamon or vanilla!
The translucent stripe on each bead is a “light window” that lets light in
Cut stem tips can be rooted in water – a fun project for children
diseases: Deflating, shrivelling pearls = too little water or diseased roots
Soft, rotting pearls = overwatering
Pale, yellow pearls = too little sun
Pearls falling off = a normal process; new ones will grow
string-of-pearls.propagation: Lay a stem on moist soil and wait – the nodes root by themselves.

string-of-hearts.name: String of hearts

care.water: Every 14–21 days, keep it on the dry side like a succulent

string-of-hearts.description: Delicate heart-shaped leaves hanging on thread-like stems! Perfect for trailing from shelves. A very fashionable and photogenic plant.
funFacts: One of the most popular “boho” houseplants of recent years
The heart-shaped leaves have purple undersides and green patterns on top
It forms small tubers (bulbils) on its stems – water storage!
It blooms with odd tube-shaped flowers that lure flies to pollinate them
The Silver Glory variety has silvery-grey leaves
diseases: Yellow leaves = overwatering – rare, but deadly
Wrinkled leaves = time to water
Pale leaves = too little light
Dropping leaves = cold or stress
string-of-hearts.propagation: Lay a stem on moist soil – it roots at the nodes. Or root cuttings in water.

aeonium.name: Black rose aeonium

care.light: Full sun – the more, the darker the leaves

aeonium.description: A dramatic rosette of dark purple to black leaves. The more sun, the darker the colour! In summer it goes dormant and may drop leaves.
funFacts: The more sun, the blacker the leaves – it's UV protection (anthocyanins)
It goes dormant in summer (aestivation) – the opposite of other succulents
In the wild it grows on sunny volcanic cliffs in the Canary Islands
It may bloom with a tall yellow flower head – after which that rosette dies
Monocarpic – each rosette flowers once in its life
diseases: Leaves fading and turning green = too little sun
Leaf drop in summer = normal summer dormancy
Rot = overwatering in winter
aeonium.propagation: Rosette cuttings – cut off, let dry for 2 days and plant in sand.

calathea.name: Calathea

care.water: Every 5–7 days, likes evenly moist soil
care.light: Partial shade to bright indirect – no sun!

calathea.description: The diva of houseplants! Painted leaves with pink stripes and purple undersides. It folds its leaves up at night (nyctinasty). It needs high humidity.
funFacts: It folds its leaves at night as if in prayer – which is why it's called a “prayer plant”
The leaves move thanks to water-filled motor cells (the pulvinus)
The purple undersides help capture light reflected from the forest floor
Very sensitive to chlorine and fluoride in tap water – use rainwater!
It rustles softly as it moves its leaves – you can hear it at night
diseases: Brown edges = dry air (the most common problem indoors)
Yellowing leaves = overwatering or hard tap water
Fading patterns = too much direct sun
Curled leaves = too cold or too dry
calathea.propagation: Divide the clump in spring. Each part must have roots and at least 2–3 leaves.

maranta.name: Prayer plant (Maranta)

care.water: Every 5–7 days, keep it lightly moist

maranta.description: The praying plant! It folds its leaves upright at night. Ornamental leaf patterns in green, burgundy and white. A cousin of calathea, but easier to care for.
funFacts: It folds its leaves upright at night – hence the name “prayer plant”
The leaf patterns are as unique as fingerprints – no two are the same
Easier to care for than calathea – more forgiving of mistakes
It blooms with tiny white flowers, but is grown mainly for its leaves
The Erythroneura variety has scarlet veins
diseases: Brown edges = dry air or fluoride in the water
Pale leaves = too much sun
Yellowing leaves = overwatering
Spider mites = webbing under the leaves from dry air – mist regularly
maranta.propagation: Divide the clump when repotting, or root stem cuttings in water.

alocasia.name: Elephant ear (Alocasia)

care.water: Every 7–10 days, likes moisture but not soggy soil

alocasia.description: Dramatic arrow-shaped leaves with contrasting white veins on a dark background. It needs high humidity, but the visual effect is worth the effort.
funFacts: Leaves can reach 60 cm long in the right conditions
New leaves emerge rolled up like parchment and unfurl within days
Under stress it goes dormant and loses its leaves – that's survival, not death
In the wild it grows in the shade of tropical forests along Asian rivers
The Polly variety is compact – ideal for small flats
diseases: Yellowing leaves = overwatering or too low a temperature
Brown edges = dry air or magnesium deficiency
Losing all its leaves = stress or winter – leave it alone, it will grow back!
Spider mites = dry air – mist and raise the humidity
alocasia.propagation: Divide the bulbs (offsets) when repotting. Each bulb with roots will give a new plant.

dieffenbachia.name: Dumb cane (Dieffenbachia)
dieffenbachia.toxic: Highly toxic – can cause loss of speech!
dieffenbachia.description: Large leaves with yellow-green patterns make it a striking office plant. WARNING: its sap contains calcium oxalate crystals that can paralyse the muscles of the mouth!
funFacts: Historically used as a punishment – people were forced to chew it and lost their speech (hence “dumb cane”)
It contains oxalate crystals that cause pain and swelling in the mouth
One of the best office plants – it tolerates poor light
It grows fast – several cm a week in good conditions
The stem can be cut at any height – it will send out new shoots
diseases: Yellow lower leaves = natural ageing or overwatering
Pale leaves = too little light
Brown spots = sunburn or cold
Stem rot = soil too wet
dieffenbachia.propagation: Stem cuttings or rooting pieces of the cane. Wear gloves!

strelitzia.name: Bird of paradise (Strelitzia)

care.water: Every 7–10 days in season, less in winter
care.light: Full sun for at least 4–6 h

strelitzia.description: An exotic flower that looks like the head of a bird of paradise! It takes years to flower indoors (5–7 years), but the sight is amazing.
funFacts: The flower looks like the head of an exotic bird with an orange crest and blue beak
Indoors it flowers after 5–7 years – it takes patience, but it's worth it
A symbol of Cape Town and South Africa
In Africa the flowers are pollinated by sunbirds that perch on the “saddle”
Its roots tolerate light drought – it dislikes soggy soil
diseases: Brown leaves = too much direct sun in a heatwave
No flowers = too little sun, too small a pot or the plant is too young
Yellowing leaves = overwatering or a nutrient deficiency
Split leaves = normal – in the wild the wind splits them so they offer less resistance
strelitzia.propagation: Division or seed (it takes months to germinate). Division is fastest but damages the roots.

caladium.name: Caladium (Angel wings)
caladium.description: Painted leaves in pinks, whites and greens! A seasonal plant – it goes dormant in winter and drops its leaves. The tuber survives and regrows in spring.
funFacts: The leaves are so thin that they glow in the sun like stained glass
In winter it loses all its leaves and rests – that's not death, it's the life cycle
There are over 1,000 varieties with different patterns and colours
It comes from the banks of the Amazon, where it grows in the shade of trees
In Vietnam and tropical Asia it's planted outdoors all year round
diseases: Wilting and dropping leaves in autumn = natural dormancy – don't throw it away!
Rotting tubers = too wet during dormancy or too cold
Brown edges = dry air or sun
No leaves appearing = tubers too cold – move to a warm spot
caladium.propagation: Divide the tubers before the season. Each tuber with an “eye” will give a new plant.

spider-plant.name: Spider plant
spider-plant.description: An unspoilt classic! Long, arching leaves and “babies” dangling on long runners. NASA TOP 10 – removes formaldehyde, carbon monoxide and benzene from the air.
funFacts: One of NASA's TOP 10 air-purifying plants
It produces baby plants (spiderettes) on long runners – perfect for giving away
Thick, fleshy roots store water – it tolerates weeks without watering
It can be kept in cultivation for over 100 years – a true heirloom
The plain green form (no stripe) is even easier than the variegated one
diseases: Brown tips = fluoride in the water or dry air
Pale leaves = too little light
Rotting roots = overwatering in cold conditions
No babies = pot too big or too little light
spider-plant.propagation: Cut off the baby plants once they have a few roots and plant them in a new pot.

tradescantia.name: Wandering dude (Tradescantia)

care.light: Bright to very bright – the colours fade in shade

tradescantia.description: The zebra of plants! Purple-silver stripes on the leaves and deep purple undersides. Grows fast and propagates easily. The more light, the more intense the colours.
funFacts: The more light, the more intense the purple of the leaves
It grows literally like crazy – several cm a week in season
The leaves are eaten in some cultures (Mexico)
The sap can cause mild skin irritation in sensitive people
One of the easiest plants to root – any sprig in water will do
diseases: Loss of purple colour = too little light
Rotting stems = overwatering
Brown leaves = frost or sunburn
tradescantia.propagation: Cuttings in water – roots within a week. One of the easiest!

peperomia.name: Peperomia (Radiator plant)
peperomia.description: The perfect miniature! Glossy, thick leaves store water. There are 1,000+ peperomia species with all kinds of leaf shapes – from round to lance-shaped.
funFacts: The genus Peperomia has over 1,000 described species – one of the largest!
Thick leaves store water like a succulent – it tolerates neglect
It blooms with long, spiky flower spikes – an exotic look
Ideal for allergy sufferers – it produces little pollen
The Watermelon variety has leaves like watermelon rind – one of the prettiest patterns
diseases: Soft, watery leaves = overwatering
Wrinkled leaves = too dry or too warm
Yellow leaves = overwatering or too large a pot
Brown spots = sunburn or bacteria
peperomia.propagation: Leaf or stem cuttings. Very easy in water or damp perlite.

ivy.name: English ivy
ivy.description: The classic European climber! It can trail, climb or sprawl. Surprisingly, it grows better in cooler rooms. One of the best air filters.
funFacts: NASA TOP 10 – one of the most effective filters of benzene and formaldehyde
In the wild it can live 400–500 years and grow a trunk as thick as a tree!
It loves COOL conditions – a warm flat is stressful for it; ideal for an unheated room
Clinging rootlets on the stem stick to walls without any support
Used since antiquity as a symbol of eternity, in victory wreaths
diseases: Spider mites = dry, warm air – move it somewhere cooler
Yellow leaves = too warm or overwatering
Greyish spots = powdery mildew from poor air circulation
Dropping leaves = warmth + dry air, or overwatering
ivy.propagation: Cuttings in water – roots within 2–3 weeks. One of the easiest.

aglaonema.name: Chinese evergreen (Aglaonema)

care.light: Tolerates deep shade – but the colours fade

aglaonema.description: A survival champion! It tolerates deep shade, poor water and forgotten waterings. Coloured varieties (red, pink, silver) look as if they were painted.
funFacts: It can grow with barely 10% of natural daylight
In Asia it's believed to bring luck and prosperity
Red and pink varieties need more light to keep their colours
One of NASA's TOP 10 air-purifying plants
It copes with office air conditioning – hence “queen of office plants”
diseases: Yellow leaves = overwatering or draught
Faded colours = too little light (especially in coloured varieties)
Brown tips = dry air or fluoride in the water
Spider mites or mealybugs = check the undersides of the leaves
aglaonema.propagation: Divide when repotting or root stem cuttings in water.

monstera-adansonii.name: Monkey mask monstera (M. adansonii)
monstera-adansonii.description: The smaller cousin of Monstera deliciosa, with leaves full of oval holes from a young age. It grows fast and looks lovely trailing or climbing a moss pole.
funFacts: Holes appear from the very first leaves – unlike M. deliciosa
It can grow up to 30 cm a month in good conditions!
In the wild it climbs trees in the tropical forests of the Americas
It roots in no time – even in a jar on the windowsill
There is also Monstera obliqua – a rare species with extremely large holes
diseases: Yellow leaves = overwatering
No holes = too little light – move it closer to the window
Brown edges = dry air
Small leaves = it needs a support to climb
monstera-adansonii.propagation: Cuttings with a node in water or sphagnum. Roots appear after 2–3 weeks.

palm-areca.name: Areca palm (Butterfly palm)

care.water: Every 5–7 days, likes slightly moist soil

palm-areca.description: The most popular indoor palm! Elegant, feathery fronds bring a tropical feel. A natural humidifier – it transpires up to 1 litre of water a day!
funFacts: It transpires up to 1 litre of water a day – a natural air humidifier
NASA TOP 10 – the best palm for purifying the air
In Madagascar (where it comes from) it is endangered!
Yellowish stems are a trait of the species, not a disease – don't worry
In the wild it grows in dense tropical forests, in light shade
diseases: Brown tips = dry air or mineral salts – repot or flush the soil
Yellow leaves = overwatering or iron deficiency
Spider mites = dry air – mist daily
Brown spots = sunburn or cold
palm-areca.propagation: Division (if it has several stems) or seed (germinates in 2–3 months).

boston-fern.name: Boston fern
boston-fern.description: The classic lush trailing fern. Perfect for the bathroom! It needs high humidity and regular watering, but rewards you with a lush, green look.
funFacts: One of the most effective air-purifying plants
Perfect for the bathroom – the naturally humid environment suits it
It can trail over a metre from a basket – striking as a hanging plant
In the wild it grows in humid tropical forests all over the world
Easy to multiply by division – after a few years it forms huge clumps
diseases: Brown, drying fronds = dry air or overwatering
Dropping fronds = draught or a sudden change in conditions
Yellowing fronds = overwatering or water that's too hard
Scale insects = brown bumps on the fronds – wipe with alcohol
boston-fern.propagation: Division or rooting the runners (stolons) – a bit like strawberries.

venus.name: Venus flytrap

care.water: ONLY rainwater or distilled water, keep constantly wet
care.light: Full sun for at least 4–6 h

venus.description: The legend of carnivorous plants! Its traps snap shut in a fraction of a second after the trigger hairs are touched twice. In the wild it grows in only one place on Earth.
funFacts: It grows naturally ONLY within 160 km of Wilmington in the Carolinas – nowhere else!
A trap closes in 0.1–0.3 seconds – one of the fastest movements in the plant kingdom
Each trap lasts only ~10 catches, then turns black and falls off
It NEEDS a winter rest at about 5°C for 3–4 months – otherwise it dies within a few years
Use ONLY rainwater or distilled water – the minerals in tap water are deadly
In the wild it grows in nitrogen-poor soil – insects are its fertiliser
diseases: Blackening traps = normal (each lasts ~10 catches) or overwatering
Traps not moving = the plant is saving energy – don't trigger them for no reason
The whole plant turns black = mineral-rich water or no winter dormancy
No growth = it needs a winter rest or more sun
venus.propagation: Division of the rhizome or leaf cuttings (slow, 3–6 months). Division is easiest.

bonsai.name: Ficus bonsai

care.light: Bright, at least a few hours of sun

bonsai.description: A miniature tree – living art! It needs regular pruning, wiring and repotting. Ficus microcarpa is one of the easiest species for bonsai.
funFacts: The art of bonsai comes from China (penjing) and reached Japan in the 8th century
Record bonsai are over 800 years old – handed down through generations
Root pruning when repotting is the key to keeping it small
Wiring the branches lets you create any shape – like sculpting living material
In Japan bonsai symbolises harmony, patience and transience
diseases: Dropping leaves = stress (new spot, draught, cold)
Yellow leaves = overwatering or too large a pot
Curled leaves = drying out or pests
Rot = poor drainage or too large a pot
bonsai.propagation: Semi-ripe cuttings with rooting hormone, or air layering.

tillandsia.name: Air plant (Tillandsia)

care.water: Soak in water for 20 min once a week

tillandsia.description: A plant without soil! It takes up water and nutrients through its leaves (trichomes). Place it on a stone, driftwood or a shell – anywhere. The most free-spirited houseplant.
funFacts: It doesn't need soil – its roots only anchor it, they don't take up water
It absorbs water and nutrients through special scales on its leaves (trichomes)
Before flowering it turns bright red or pink – a signal for hummingbirds
After flowering the mother plant dies, but leaves offsets behind
You can glue it to wood, stone or glass – complete creative freedom
diseases: Brown, dry leaves = too little water or air too dry
Rotting centre = too much water or not drying out after soaking
Curled leaves = too dry
tillandsia.propagation: Separate the offsets (pups) once they reach half the size of the mother plant.

coffee.name: Arabian coffee plant
coffee.toxic: Seeds and leaves mildly toxic to pets
coffee.description: Grow your own coffee! After a few years it blooms with white, jasmine-scented flowers, then produces red cherries with coffee beans inside.
funFacts: It comes from Ethiopia – legend tells of Kaldi's goats dancing after eating the berries
It blooms with small white flowers with an intense jasmine scent
The red cherries take 9 months to ripen – each contains 2 coffee beans
One houseplant may produce a handful of coffee a year – but the satisfaction is priceless
Arabica is the finer species – grown on 60% of the world's plantations
diseases: Yellowing leaves = too much sun or iron deficiency
Dropping leaves = stress, draught or too dry
Brown spots = sunburn
No growth = winter rest – normal
coffee.propagation: From seed (fresh beans taken from the cherry) or stem cuttings. Seeds take 1–2 months to germinate.

mimosa.name: Sensitive plant (Mimosa pudica)
mimosa.description: The touchy plant! It folds its leaflets the moment you touch it and opens them again after a few minutes. It's an evolutionary way to deter plant-eaters.
funFacts: The touch signal travels through the plant at about 4 cm per second – faster than you'd think
It opens its leaves in the morning and folds them by itself in the evening (nyctinasty)
Studies show it can “learn” – after many harmless touches it stops reacting
Charles Darwin studied it as one of the first plants showing sense-like behaviour
It blooms with pink pompoms that look like tiny hedgehogs
diseases: Leaves not folding when touched = the plant is saving energy or is unwell
Yellow leaves = overwatering or lack of nutrients
Dropping leaves = cold or stress
mimosa.propagation: From seed. Soak overnight in warm water and sow in a warm spot.

oxalis.name: Purple shamrock (Oxalis)
oxalis.description: Triangular purple leaflets fold and open in a daily rhythm. It goes dormant in summer and regrows from its bulbs. One of the prettiest easy plants.
funFacts: It folds its leaves at night and on cloudy days – it has its own body clock
Delicate pink flowers contrast with the dark purple leaves
It comes from Brazil, where it grows in shady places
It goes dormant in summer – don't throw it away when it loses its leaves, it will regrow!
The purple colour comes from anthocyanins – the same as in blueberries
diseases: Losing leaves in summer = normal summer dormancy
Stretched shoots = too little light
Rotting bulbs = too wet during dormancy
oxalis.propagation: Divide the bulbs. Each bulb will give a new plant within a few weeks.

citrus.name: Meyer lemon

care.light: Full sun – at least 8 h a day or a grow light

citrus.description: A lemon in a pot! The Meyer variety is sweeter and hardier than an ordinary lemon. It flowers fragrantly and bears edible fruit after 1–3 years.
funFacts: The Meyer lemon is a cross between a lemon and a mandarin – which is why it's sweeter
In good conditions it flowers and fruits all year round
The flowers have an intense, exotic scent – notes of orange and jasmine
In China it has been grown for centuries in pots by entrances as a symbol of luck
One of the best fruits to grow at home – a real harvest in a flat
diseases: Dropping leaves = stress (new spot, cold, draught)
Yellowing leaves = iron deficiency or water too hard
No fruit = too little sun or no pollination (shake the branches)
Aphids on new shoots = common – a jet of water or soapy water
citrus.propagation: Semi-ripe cuttings or grafting onto a rootstock.

venus-flytrapper.name: Sundew (Drosera)

care.water: ONLY rainwater or distilled water; keep it in a tray that's always wet
care.light: Full sun for at least 4 h

venus-flytrapper.description: Carnivorous elegance! Red tentacles covered with sticky dew catch insects. One of the easiest carnivorous plants – perfect for beginners.
funFacts: The red droplets aren't dew – they're sticky mucilage that lures insects
The leaf slowly curls around its prey over several days
One of the easiest carnivorous plants – a good start in carnivores
It tolerates low temperatures – you can put it on the balcony for the summer
Use ONLY rainwater – the minerals in tap water kill it within months
diseases: Blackening leaves = normal ageing or minerals in the water
No sticky droplets = too little sun or air too dry
Rot = the wrong substrate (use peat and perlite)
venus-flytrapper.propagation: Leaf cuttings on a peat–perlite mix. Seeds.

pothos-neon.name: Neon pothos

care.light: Bright – the more light, the more neon the colour!

pothos-neon.description: A fluorescent pothos variety with intensely lime, almost glowing leaves. The colour intensifies in strong light.
funFacts: The more bright light, the more intense the neon colour of the leaves
In shade the leaves turn greener and lose their neon tone – it needs more light than ordinary pothos
It's a sport of the same species as Golden pothos – the difference is in its pigments
One of the trendiest Instagram plants – it looks like it's from another planet
diseases: Fading colour = too little light – move it to a brighter window
Yellow leaves = overwatering
Brown tips = dry air
pothos-neon.propagation: Just like Golden pothos – cuttings with nodes in water.

rhipsalis.name: Mistletoe cactus (Rhipsalis)
rhipsalis.origin: Tropical Americas (the only cactus also found wild in Africa!)

care.light: Bright indirect to partial shade – NOT full sun (it's a forest cactus!)

rhipsalis.description: A forest cactus without spines! Its trailing, thread-like stems look like underwater coral. The only member of the cactus family that grows wild outside the Americas.
funFacts: The only cactus that grows wild outside the Americas – also found in Africa and Sri Lanka
A forest cactus – unlike other cacti it does NOT need full sun, it likes shade!
It blooms with tiny white flowers followed by pearly berries
The berries have sticky juice – birds eat them and spread the seeds
Perfect as a hanging plant – its stems trail a metre or more
diseases: Red or orange stems = sunburn or water stress
Segments falling off = stress (too dry or too wet)
Shrivelling stems = too dry
rhipsalis.propagation: Stem cuttings – cut a segment, let it dry for a day and insert it into moist peat.

fittonia.name: Nerve plant (Fittonia)

care.water: Every 5–7 days, keep moist – NOT wet

fittonia.description: A network of veins on miniature leaves – green leaves with white, pink or red veins. It droops dramatically without water but bounces back after watering.
funFacts: The leaf veins can be white, pink or red – a natural work of art
It droops dramatically when thirsty – even more of a drama queen than the peace lily!
Perfect for terrariums – it loves a humid, enclosed environment
In a terrarium it can go months without watering!
It comes from the humid forests of the Amazon, beside rain-fed streams
diseases: Drooping = it needs water – water it and it recovers quickly
Rotting stems = too much water
Brown spots = water too hard or sun
Pale leaves = too much sun
fittonia.propagation: Stem cuttings in water – roots appear after 1–2 weeks.

syngonium.name: Arrowhead plant (Syngonium)
syngonium.description: Its arrow-shaped leaves change shape with age! Young ones are compact, older ones split into “fingers”. Dozens of coloured varieties.
funFacts: The leaf shape changes dramatically with age – young ones are arrows, old ones have “fingers”
There are 30+ colour varieties – pink, white, green, mint
It can be grown trailing or climbing
The Albo-Variegatum variety has white and green patches – every leaf looks different
diseases: Yellow lower leaves = natural ageing or overwatering
Brown spots = sunburn or water too hard
Pale colours = too little light
syngonium.propagation: Stem cuttings with a node in water – roots within 1–2 weeks.

polka-dot.name: Polka dot plant (Hypoestes)
polka-dot.description: Leaves speckled like a ladybird! Pink, white or red dots on a green background. It grows fast and fills out plant arrangements beautifully.
funFacts: The more bright light, the more intense and distinct the dots
It produces small lavender flowers – a pretty accent
It comes from Madagascar – one of the islands richest in endemic species
Ideal for mixed arrangements and terrariums
diseases: Pale, fading dots = too little light
Rotting stems = overwatering
Dropping leaves = cold or draught
polka-dot.propagation: Stem cuttings in water – very easy.

zz-raven.name: ZZ Raven (Black ZZ plant)
zz-raven.origin: Cultivar of an East African plant
zz-raven.description: The gothic version of the classic ZZ plant! New leaves emerge bright green, then darken to an almost black purple. A striking live transformation.
funFacts: New leaves come out bright green and gradually darken to almost black!
The colour changes over several weeks – you can watch the transformation
It only reached the market around 2019 – one of the “new” black plants
The same survival skills as the ordinary ZZ – indestructible
diseases: Yellow leaves = overwatering (just like the ordinary ZZ)
Leaves staying green instead of turning black = too little light
zz-raven.propagation: Rhizome division or leaf cuttings (6–12 months).

bromeliad.name: Bromeliad (Guzmania)

care.water: Water into the rosette (cup) once a week, keep the soil almost dry

bromeliad.description: A spectacular bloom that lasts for months! The “flower” is actually coloured leaves surrounding tiny flowers. After flowering the mother plant dies but leaves “babies”.
funFacts: The pineapple is a bromeliad too – it belongs to the same family!
The flower head is made of coloured leaves (bracts), not petals
Pour water into the “cup” in the centre of the rosette – that's how rain waters it in the wild
The mother plant dies after flowering – a normal cycle, not a care mistake
Offset rosettes can be separated and grown into new plants – they flower after 2–3 years
diseases: Rotting base = soil too wet or water left standing too long
Browning flower head = the natural end of flowering after 2–6 months
Pale colours = too little bright light
bromeliad.propagation: Separate the offsets (pups) once they reach 1/3 of the mother plant's size.

bird-nest-fern.name: Bird's nest fern
bird-nest-fern.description: Glossy, wavy fronds grow from a central rosette like a bird's nest. One of the most beautiful ferns for interiors – it looks like a sculpture.
funFacts: In the wild it grows on trees as an epiphyte – its “nest” collects fallen leaves as fertiliser
Young fronds are coiled like fiddleheads – delicate and beautiful
Never pour water straight into the centre of the rosette – it causes rot
Resistant to insects – in the wild few things attack it
Available in varieties with very wavy or crinkled frond edges
diseases: Brown edges = air too dry – mist the fronds
Yellow fronds = overwatering or too much sun
Black spots = water in the rosette and rot – water the soil only
bird-nest-fern.propagation: Only from spores – slow and difficult. Easiest to buy a new plant.

schefflera.name: Umbrella tree (Schefflera)

care.water: Every 7–10 days, once the top is dry

schefflera.description: Elegant hand-shaped leaves arranged like an umbrella. It grows quickly into a small tree. It tolerates neglect but likes regular watering and a bright spot.
funFacts: Its compound leaves have 7–9 leaflets fanned out – hence the umbrella name
In the wild it reaches 4 m and grows as a hedge or small tree
It can be trained as a bonsai – its flexible stems are easy to braid
The variegated form has yellow-green leaves – more striking
diseases: Dropping leaves = stress (moving house, draught)
Yellow leaves = overwatering or too little light
Brown tips = dry air

palm-kentia.name: Kentia palm

care.light: From partial shade to bright – one of the few palms that tolerate shade

palm-kentia.description: The regal palm of offices and hotels. One of the few palms that tolerate shade and central heating. It grows slowly but lives for decades.
funFacts: It grows naturally only on tiny Lord Howe Island in the Pacific – an endemic!
Found in Europe's hotels and palaces since the 19th century – a symbol of elegance
One of the few palms that tolerate deep shade and dry air
Slow growth – 30–60 cm a year, but it lives for decades
In the wild it reaches 18 m – indoors it stays small
diseases: Brown tips = dry air or salt in the soil
Yellowing lower fronds = natural ageing (1–2 a year is normal)
Spider mites = dry environment – mist regularly
palm-kentia.propagation: Seeds take 2–3 months to germinate. Division isn't possible – it has a single trunk.

basil.name: Basil

care.light: Full sun for at least 6 h

basil.description: The king of Mediterranean cooking! Fresh leaves are most aromatic in the morning, before the heat. Pinch out the tips regularly to make it bushy and delay flowering.
funFacts: The word “basil” comes from the Greek “basilikos” – royal
Flowering = the end of the aroma – right after flowering the leaves turn bitter
There are 60+ varieties: Thai, lemon, chocolate, purple...
It releases compounds that repel flies and mosquitoes – a natural repellent
In ancient Egypt it was used in mummification
It tastes best fresh – cooking destroys the essential oils
diseases: Black spots on leaves = downy mildew or a chill
Wilting = too dry or too hot
Yellow leaves = overwatering or too large a pot
Brown edges = cold air or a draught
basil.propagation: Cuttings in water – roots after 1–2 weeks. Or seeds – they germinate in 5–7 days in the warmth.

mint.name: Peppermint
mint.description: Unstoppable! It spreads by rhizomes in every direction. Plant it in a pot even in the garden. Ideal for teas, cocktails and cooking.
funFacts: The menthol in its leaves activates cold receptors – hence the cooling feeling
It spreads so aggressively it can take over a whole garden in 2 seasons
A natural repellent – mosquitoes and mice dislike the smell of mint
Peppermint is a hybrid – it doesn't exist in the wild, only as a cultivated plant
Mint tea has an antispasmodic effect on the digestive system
There are about 25 mint species, plus apple, chocolate and pineapple mints...
diseases: Rust on the leaves = fungus – remove the affected leaves, improve air flow
Aphids = on young shoots – blast them off with water
Rotting roots = overwatering
Bleached leaves = too much direct sun
mint.propagation: Cuttings in water – roots after a week. Division of the rhizomes. One of the easiest.

rosemary.name: Rosemary

care.water: Every 7–14 days, drought-tolerant like a succulent
care.light: Full sun for at least 6 h

rosemary.description: A herb that becomes a shrub! It turns woody with age and tolerates drought like a succulent. Aromatic needle-like leaves all year round. Its lavender-blue flowers are loved by pollinators.
funFacts: The name comes from the Latin “ros marinus” – dew of the sea
In antiquity it was a symbol of memory – students wore garlands of it to exams
Rosemary oil improves blood circulation in the scalp
It tolerates frost down to -10°C – hardy outdoors in winter
It can live 30+ years and turn into a decorative little tree
The flowers are edible – great for decorating salads
diseases: Powdery mildew = air too humid – improve air flow
Rotting roots = overwatering (the main killer!)
Yellowing leaves = soil too wet
Dry tips = normal in winter, it grows slowly
rosemary.propagation: Semi-ripe cuttings (10 cm) in sand. Roots after 3–4 weeks.

lavender.name: Lavender
lavender.description: The scent of Provence in a pot! Purple flower spikes in summer. Dried, they keep their aroma for years. A natural moth and mosquito repellent.
funFacts: Known for 2,500 years – the Romans used it in their baths (Latin lavare = to wash)
Dried flowers keep their scent for 2–3 years
Lavender is one of the most popular aromatherapy plants in the world
A natural moth repellent – lavender sachets in the wardrobe
Lavender honey is among the most prized honeys in the world
Lavender oil is calming – used in aromatherapy for insomnia
diseases: Grey mould = too damp, too little air
Rotting roots = soil too wet – overwatering
Woody stems without leaves = pot too small or old plant – prune it
No flowers = too little sun
lavender.propagation: Tip cuttings of 8 cm without a flower. Roots after 3–4 weeks.

chives.name: Chives
chives.description: The fastest kitchen herb! After cutting it grows back within a week. Never cut more than 1/3 at a time. The purple flowers are edible too.
funFacts: It regrows in no time – you can cut it every 2–3 weeks all year round
The flowers are edible – a pretty salad decoration with a mild onion taste
One of the classic “fines herbes” of French cuisine
Used for over 5,000 years – one of the oldest cultivated herbs
It deters aphids – a great companion plant
diseases: Rust = brown spots on the leaves – remove the affected ones, improve air flow
Powdery mildew = white fuzz – too damp
Yellowing leaves = too little nitrogen or too large a pot
chives.propagation: Divide the clump every 2–3 years. Seeds – they germinate after 10–14 days.

aloe-arborescens.name: Candelabra aloe
aloe-arborescens.description: The bigger and tougher sibling of aloe vera! In Japan it's called “Kidachi aloe” (tree aloe). Similar medicinal properties, but much hardier and more impressive.
funFacts: In Japan it's called “isha-irazu” – “no need for a doctor”
Studied for its potential anti-cancer properties since the 1980s
It blooms with striking orange flower spikes in winter
Frost-hardy down to -5°C – it can go outdoors in summer
It produces more gel than aloe vera relative to its size
diseases: Brown, soft leaves = overwatering
Red leaves = sun or water stress – normal
Wrinkled leaves = time to water
aloe-arborescens.propagation: Separate the side rosettes. Let them dry for 2 days and plant.

cactus-opuntia.name: Prickly pear (Opuntia)

care.water: Every 3–4 weeks, more often in summer

cactus-opuntia.description: A cactus with edible fruit and pads! The fruit (tuna) is sweet, and the pads (nopales) are edible once the spines are removed. A symbol of Mexico – it's on the flag!
funFacts: It has been on Mexico's coat of arms and flag for 700 years
The pads (nopales) are a popular vegetable in Mexican cuisine
The fruit (cactus pear) is rich in vitamin C
The cochineal insect lives on opuntia – it's the source of carmine (E120)
It tolerates temperatures from -10°C to +50°C – exceptional hardiness
In the wild it forms impenetrable thickets – a natural “fence”
diseases: Brown, soft pads = overwatering
Yellow, shrivelling pads = too little water or too cold
White waxy coating = normal (protective wax) or mealybugs
cactus-opuntia.propagation: Cut off a pad, let it dry for 5–7 days until the wound seals, then plant in sand.

cactus-cereus.name: Column cactus (Cereus)

care.water: Every 3–4 weeks, not at all in winter

cactus-cereus.description: The classic column cactus – it grows straight up like a green pillar. One of the fastest-growing cacti. After many years it blooms with huge white flowers at night.
funFacts: It blooms only at night – the flowers open after dark and wilt before sunrise
Each flower lives for just one night – but it's huge (15–20 cm)
In the wild it reaches 10 m and lives 200+ years
One of the fastest-growing cacti – up to 30 cm a year in the sun
The fruit (pitaya) is edible – sweet and pinkish-red
diseases: Browning base = rot from overwatering – critical!
Wrinkling = too little water in summer
Yellowing = too little sun or too cold
cactus-cereus.propagation: Cut off a 10 cm tip, let it dry for a week, then plant in sand.

cactus-mammillaria.name: Pincushion cactus (Mammillaria)

care.water: Every 2–3 weeks, not at all in winter

cactus-mammillaria.description: A cactus with a crown of flowers! Every spring it forms a ring of small pink or yellow flowers around its top. One of the easiest cacti to bring into bloom.
funFacts: It blooms every year with a ring of flowers around the top – like a tiara
The genus Mammillaria has 200+ species – one of the largest in the cactus family
Its spines are arranged in Fibonacci spirals – mathematics in nature
Frost-hardy down to -5°C – it can go outside in summer
After flowering it forms red berries – edible!
diseases: Rotting base = overwatering – the main cause of death
No flowers = too little sun or too warm a winter
Mealybugs = white fluff between the spines – wipe with alcohol
cactus-mammillaria.propagation: Separate the side offsets, let them dry for 2 days and plant.

cactus-gymnocalycium.name: Moon cactus (Gymnocalycium)

care.light: Bright indirect – an exception among cacti!

cactus-gymnocalycium.description: A cactus without chlorophyll! The “moon cactus” is a red or yellow ball grafted onto a green rootstock. With no chlorophyll, it lives off the rootstock's photosynthesis.
funFacts: The moon cactus has no chlorophyll and is grafted onto Hylocereus – it lives on its rootstock's “blood”
The red, yellow and orange colours are pigments no longer masked by chlorophyll
One of the most popular plants in Japanese garden shops
The rootstock can outlive the grafted top – you can graft a new one
It tolerates partial shade – an exception among sun-loving cacti
diseases: Fading colour = too little or too much sun
Rotting rootstock = overwatering
Shrinking = too dry or a failing graft
cactus-gymnocalycium.propagation: Graft offset balls onto a new Hylocereus rootstock.

monstera-thai.name: Monstera Thai Constellation

care.light: Bright indirect – key for the patterns!

monstera-thai.description: The world's most expensive monstera! Creamy-white speckles and streaks on its leaves like a constellation. A genetic mutation that arose in a Thai laboratory – it doesn't exist in the wild.
funFacts: It arose as a chance mutation in a Thai tissue-culture lab in the 1990s
At the peak of the craze (2021) a single plant cost USD 5,000–20,000!
The pattern on each leaf is unique – no two leaves look alike
It grows slowly because the white areas have little chlorophyll
The white/cream areas can't photosynthesise – the green parts have to “feed” the whole plant
Prices have returned to normal – it's now affordable
diseases: Changing patterns = normal variation – every leaf is different
Yellow leaves = overwatering
Brown spots = dry air or sunburn
Slow growth = normal with low chlorophyll
monstera-thai.propagation: Cuttings with a node – just like an ordinary monstera. The patterns aren't always passed on.

philodendron-pink.name: Philodendron Pink Princess

care.light: Bright indirect – needed for the pink!

philodendron-pink.description: The pink princess! Dark green leaves with pink or cream patches. The patterns are genetically unstable – every leaf is a surprise.
funFacts: The pink colour comes from a lack of chlorophyll in those areas (like Thai Constellation)
In 2020–2021 it sold for USD 1,000–5,000 per plant!
The patterns are genetically unstable – it can “revert” to plain green
Strong light helps keep the pink and produce more variegated leaves
The “Dark Lord” variety has almost black leaves with no pattern – a moody alternative
diseases: Fading pink patterns = too little light or reversion – give it more light
Yellow leaves = overwatering
Brown tips = dry air
philodendron-pink.propagation: Cuttings with a node in water or sphagnum. The patterns are partly passed on.

anthurium-warocqueanum.name: Queen anthurium
anthurium-warocqueanum.description: The queen of anthuriums! Huge velvety leaves up to 1 m long with distinct silvery veins. It needs very high humidity – a typical greenhouse plant.
funFacts: Its leaves can reach 100 cm long in ideal conditions
The velvety texture comes from microscopic projections on the leaf surface
Considered one of the most difficult houseplants – a real challenge
In Colombia it grows in cloud forests at 80–90% humidity
A rare collector's plant – prices from hundreds to thousands
diseases: Brown edges and tips = air too dry (the most common problem!)
Yellowing leaves = overwatering or too low a temperature
Slow growth = conditions too dry or too cold
anthurium-warocqueanum.propagation: Division or side offsets. Needs a terrarium or greenhouse while propagating.

scindapsus-pictus.name: Satin pothos (Scindapsus pictus)
scindapsus-pictus.description: The silver pothos! Matte, dark green leaves with silvery splashes like spilt silver. As easy as pothos but more striking. Very fashionable in interior design.
funFacts: Often confused with pothos, but it belongs to a different genus
The silver patches are air pockets in the leaf that reflect light
The Argyraeus variety has smaller, more densely speckled leaves
The Exotica variety has larger, more contrasting silver patterns
One of the trendiest plants on Instagram since 2022
diseases: Yellow leaves = overwatering
Fading patterns = too little light
Brown tips = dry air
scindapsus-pictus.propagation: Cuttings with a node in water. Roots appear after 2–3 weeks.

dischidia.name: Ant plant (Dischidia)
dischidia.description: The ant plant! In the wild it forms special hollow leaves – little “houses” where ants live. Trailing chains of small round leaves like coins.
funFacts: In the wild it forms hollow pouch leaves where ants live – mutualism!
The ants protect the plant and fertilise the special leaves with their waste
Related to hoya – similar needs and looks
The Million Hearts variety has densely packed heart-shaped leaves
An epiphyte – in the wild it grows on trees, not in soil
diseases: Wrinkled leaves = too dry
Rotting stems = overwatering
Brown tips = dry air
dischidia.propagation: Stem cuttings in water or sphagnum.

burros-tail.name: Burro's tail (Donkey's tail)

care.light: Bright with a few hours of sun

burros-tail.description: A thick, trailing “tail” made of hundreds of small fleshy leaves. It looks like a braid of juicy pearls. Very decorative in a hanging basket or on a shelf.
funFacts: The leaves are attached so loosely that they fall off at the slightest touch
Every fallen leaf can grow into a new plant – lay it on sand and wait
A fully grown stem can trail 60–90 cm
It blooms with small pink flowers at the stem tips
One of the most striking succulents for hanging baskets
diseases: Leaves dropping when touched = normal! Avoid handling
Wrinkled leaves = too little water
Rotting base = overwatering
burros-tail.propagation: Lay fallen leaves on dry sand – new rosettes appear after 2–4 weeks.

columnea.name: Goldfish plant (Columnea)
columnea.description: A goldfish in a pot! Trailing stems covered with small fleshy leaves and striking tubular flowers shaped like a goldfish's mouth.
funFacts: The flowers look like goldfish mouths – hence the name “goldfish plant”
It flowers for many months in the right light
In the wild it grows on rainforest trees as an epiphyte
There are 200+ Columnea species with different flower colours
Related to African violets and episcias – the same family (Gesneriaceae)
diseases: No flowers = too little light or too warm
Dropping leaves = draught or a sudden temperature change
Rotting stems = overwatering
columnea.propagation: Stem cuttings of 10 cm in damp perlite.

lipstick-plant.name: Lipstick plant
lipstick-plant.description: Flowers emerging from dark sheaths like lipstick from a tube! The bright red flowers are exceptionally striking. Its trailing stems are perfect for hanging baskets.
funFacts: The flowers emerge from dark tubes like lipstick from its case – hence the name
In the wild it's pollinated by sunbirds that push their beaks into the tube
It flowers profusely in bright light with cooler nights
Related to episcias and columneas – the Gesneriaceae family
There is a variety with curly, twisted leaves – Twister
diseases: No flowers = too little light or nights too warm
Bud drop = a sudden change in conditions
Yellow leaves = overwatering
lipstick-plant.propagation: Stem cuttings of 10 cm in damp perlite.

olive-tree.name: Olive tree

care.light: Full sun for at least 6 h – a must!

olive-tree.description: The tree of the Mediterranean in a pot! Silvery-grey leaves and a gnarled trunk with age. It may fruit after a few years. A symbol of peace and longevity.
funFacts: Olive trees live for thousands of years – the oldest are over 3,000 years old!
A symbol of peace, wisdom and victory since antiquity
It needs a cool winter rest (5–10°C) to set fruit
Indoors it can fruit 3–5 years after planting
The silvery colour of the leaves comes from tiny scales that reflect excess sun
Traditionally used for bonsai because of its trunk texture
diseases: Yellowing leaves = soil too wet or too little sun
Dropping leaves = stress (moving, cold)
No fruit = no winter rest or no pollinator
olive-tree.propagation: Semi-ripe cuttings in summer with rooting hormone.

adenium.name: Desert rose (Adenium)

care.water: Every 14–21 days, not at all in winter

adenium.description: The beauty of the desert! Its thick, bottle-shaped trunk stores water. It blooms spectacularly with pink or red flowers like an oleander. A popular bonsai in Asia.
funFacts: Its thick trunk (caudex) can store water through months of drought
In Asia (Thailand, China) it has been grown as a lucky bonsai for centuries
The poison in its milky sap was traditionally used on arrow tips
It blooms heavily during drought – stress triggers flowering
It can live for centuries – some specimens are over 300 years old
There are thousands of hybrids with different flower colours and shapes
diseases: Rotting trunk = overwatering in winter (a fatal mistake!)
Leaf drop in winter = normal dormancy
No flowers = too little sun or too cool

ficus-ginseng.name: Ginseng ficus
ficus-ginseng.description: A bonsai with bulbous roots like a fairy-tale character! Its thick, bulbous trunk (actually a root) is a striking feature. Popular in shops as a ready-made bonsai.
funFacts: The thick trunk is a modified root grown especially for decoration
In Asia it's a symbol of longevity and wisdom – a gift for important occasions
Small leaves and balanced proportions make it ideal for bonsai
Mass-produced in China and Thailand – hence the low price
It can be shaped freely by pruning and wiring
diseases: Dropping leaves = stress (new spot, draught, cold)
Yellow leaves = overwatering or air too dry
Small leaves and no growth = too few nutrients or too small a pot

staghorn-fern.name: Staghorn fern
staghorn-fern.description: An epiphyte that grows on a wall! It has two types of fronds: brown shields (for clinging) and green antlers (for show). Mounted on a board or bark like a living picture on the wall.
funFacts: It doesn't grow in soil – it's mounted on a board or bark like a picture
It has two types of fronds: shields (brown, clinging) and antlers (green, decorative)
The brown shields collect fallen leaves and humus as fertiliser – don't remove them!
You water it by soaking the whole board in water for 15–20 minutes
In the wild it grows on trees in Australia's rainforests
diseases: Browning shields = normal – part of the life cycle, don't remove them!
Black spots on the antlers = fungus from too much water
Pale, limp antlers = too little light
staghorn-fern.propagation: Separate offset plants with a shield when remounting.

selaginella.name: Peacock spikemoss (Selaginella)

care.water: Keep constantly moist – a deep tray of water

selaginella.description: Rainbow moss! Its leaves shimmer with a metallic blue-green sheen like an oil slick on water. Perfect for a terrarium – that's where it looks its best.
funFacts: The metallic sheen comes from nanostructures in its cells that refract light – like butterfly wings
It's a living fossil – its relatives grew 400 million years ago
In a closed terrarium it can go months without watering
It comes from the humid forests of China and Vietnam
In a fully sealed terrarium it forms a fairy-tale miniature forest
diseases: Browning = air too dry or too much sun
Rot = standing water at the base
Loss of sheen = conditions too dry
selaginella.propagation: Stem cuttings in damp moss or a terrarium.

nerve-plant-red.name: Red nerve plant (Fittonia)
nerve-plant-red.description: A network of red veins on dark green leaves – it looks like blood vessels under a microscope. A variety with a vivid red vein pattern.
funFacts: The leaf veins can be white, pink or scarlet – bred for colour
The perfect partner for green fittonia – together they make a contrasting display
In a terrarium it grows lushly with almost no care
It droops dramatically when thirsty – but bounces back 15 minutes after watering
Miniature varieties have leaves the size of a fingernail – ideal for nano terrariums
diseases: Drooping = it needs water – water it quickly
Rotting stems = too wet
Pale leaves = too much sun
nerve-plant-red.propagation: Stem cuttings in water – very easy.

pachira.name: Money tree (Pachira)
pachira.description: The braided money tree! Five stems are woven into a characteristic braid. In feng shui a symbol of wealth and good fortune. Its seeds are edible – they taste like nuts.
funFacts: The braided trunk is 3–5 young stems artificially woven together
Legend: a Taiwanese farmer braided 5 plants and grew rich – a myth that conquered Asia
The seeds are edible and taste like chestnuts or peanuts – they can be roasted
In the wild it grows in tropical swamp forests
A symbol of luck, wealth and success in Asian cultures
It tolerates waterlogged roots – a popular houseplant with a swampy homeland
diseases: Yellow leaves = overwatering or too cold
Dropping leaves = stress (new spot)
Brown tips = dry air or salt in the soil
pachira.propagation: Cuttings or seeds. The stems are braided by hand when they are about 1 cm thick.

nepenthes.name: Tropical pitcher plant (Nepenthes)

care.water: ONLY rainwater; keep moist; never fill the pitchers yourself!

nepenthes.description: A carnivore with pitchers! Modified leaves form pitcher traps filled with digestive fluid. It catches insects – and in the wild even small mammals!
funFacts: The pitchers are modified leaf tips filled with digestive enzymes
Large species can digest rats, frogs and even small birds!
Special spiders and fly larvae that resist the enzymes live inside the pitchers
The pitcher produces its own wax and enzymes – self-sufficient
N. × ventrata is a hybrid of two species – easier to grow than pure species
Use ONLY rainwater or distilled water – just like the Venus flytrap
diseases: Drying pitchers = air too dry or stress
Blackening leaves = too cold or overwatering
No pitchers = too little light or conditions too dry
nepenthes.propagation: Tip cuttings in sphagnum under plastic. Slow to root.

yucca.name: Spineless yucca (Yucca elephantipes)
yucca.description: A desert tree in your living room! Tough, pointed leaves grow from a thick trunk. Almost indestructible – it tolerates neglect, dry air and infrequent watering.
funFacts: In the wild yuccas are pollinated only by yucca moths (coevolution!)
It can bloom with spikes of white flowers in the right light
A cut trunk will sprout new shoots from the side – it can be pruned
Native Americans used yucca leaves to make ropes, baskets and fabric
The root contains saponins – it was used as a natural shampoo
diseases: Brown tips = normal or dry air
Soft stem at the base = overwatering and root rot
Yellow lower leaves = natural ageing
yucca.propagation: Cut off a 15 cm top, let it dry for 2 days and plant. Or separate the side shoots.

bromeliaceae-neoregelia.name: Blushing bromeliad (Neoregelia)

care.water: Water into the rosette (cup) + keep the substrate lightly moist
care.light: Bright to very bright – brings out intense colours

bromeliaceae-neoregelia.description: A bromeliad in colour! The centre of the rosette turns intense red or pink before flowering. Decorative for a long time – the coloured centre lasts for months.
funFacts: The centre of the rosette turns red a few months before flowering
The more sun, the more intense the colours of the leaves and centre
Pour water into the “cup” in the middle – that's how bromeliads take up moisture in the wild
The stripes on the leaves can be yellow, pink or cream in some varieties
The mother plant dies after flowering, but leaves many offsets
diseases: Rotting centre = water left standing too long – change it weekly
Pale colours = too little light
Brown tips = dry air
bromeliaceae-neoregelia.propagation: Separate the offsets once they reach 1/3 of the mother plant's size.

hoya-kerrii.name: Sweetheart hoya (Hoya kerrii)
hoya-kerrii.description: The love plant! Its fleshy heart-shaped leaves are a natural symbol of love. Sold as a single leaf it makes a cute decoration – but it will never grow into a full plant.
funFacts: A single leaf without a node will NEVER grow into a full plant – it's a botanical curiosity
To get a full plant you need a cutting with a piece of stem and a node
After a few years it blooms beautifully with flower clusters – they smell of chocolate!
One of the most popular Valentine's Day plants in the world
As a climber it can live for decades and reach several metres
diseases: Wrinkled leaves = too dry
Yellow leaves = overwatering
No growth = normal for a single leaf without a node
hoya-kerrii.propagation: Only cuttings with a node give a full plant. A single leaf will root but won't grow.

begonia-boliviensis.name: Bolivian begonia
begonia-boliviensis.description: A cascade of orange flowers! Trailing stems covered with dozens of narrow, tubular flowers all summer long. Ideal for hanging baskets on the balcony.
funFacts: It blooms from spring to late autumn – one of the longest-flowering begonias
In the wild it grows on rocky Andean cliffs at 1,000–2,000 m
Its tubular flowers are adapted to pollination by hummingbirds
A hanging-basket plant that loves temperate summers
It goes dormant in winter – store the tuber somewhere cool and dry
diseases: Flower drop = too dry or too hot
Powdery mildew = humid air with no circulation
Yellow leaves = overwatering
begonia-boliviensis.propagation: Stem cuttings or dividing the tubers in spring.

pilea_cadierei.name: Aluminium plant (Pilea cadierei)

care.water: Every 5–7 days, once the top of the soil is dry

pilea_cadierei.description: An attractive plant with dark green leaves and metallic silver patches. Ideal for beginners – easy and rewarding.
funFacts: Also known as the aluminium plant or watermelon pilea
The patches on the leaves are a special structure that reflects light
It propagates easily – cuttings root in water
After a few years it loses its looks – worth propagating and renewing
Safe for cats and dogs
In Vietnam it grows wild in damp forests
diseases: Drooping leaves = too dry or overwatered (check the soil)
Fading patches = too little light
Brown edges = low air humidity
Long stems = too little light, the plant is stretching
Yellow lower leaves = natural ageing or overwatering
pilea_cadierei.propagation: Tip cuttings of 10 cm – root them in water or straight into soil under plastic.

calathea_orbifolia.name: Calathea orbifolia
calathea_orbifolia.description: The most spectacular calathea – huge round leaves with distinct silver stripes. Demanding, but unforgettable.
funFacts: Its leaves can be 30 cm across
One of the “prayer plants” – in the evening it raises its leaves
Safe for cats and dogs
Very sensitive to chlorine – use water left to stand, or rainwater
In the wild it grows on the shady floor of the rainforest
It needs stable conditions – changes don't suit it
diseases: Brown tips = hard water or low humidity
Curling leaves = too little water or a draught
Yellow leaves = overwatering
Leaves permanently drooping = a root problem
Faded patterns = too much light
calathea_orbifolia.propagation: Only by dividing the clump when repotting – stem cuttings don't root.

petroselinum.name: Parsley

care.light: Bright, a few hours of sun a day
