petroselinum.description: A classic kitchen herb grown for its leaves or root. In a pot on the kitchen windowsill it gives you a fresh addition to meals all year round.
funFacts: A biennial – in its second year it flowers and dies
Rich in vitamin C – more than lemon per 100 g
In ancient Greece it symbolised death – it was planted on graves
A natural breath freshener after eating garlic
It grows best in a kitchen that's cooler than the living room
Freshly cut, it lasts 1–2 weeks in water
diseases: Yellow leaves = lack of nutrients (nitrogen)
Limp leaves = lack of water
Whitish coating = powdery mildew – ventilate
Flower stalk = second year of life, natural
Aphids – rinse off with soapy water
petroselinum.propagation: From seed – germinates slowly (3–4 weeks). Better to buy a potted plant or sow several times a season.

thymus_vulgaris.name: Thyme

care.water: Every 5–7 days, let the soil dry out between waterings
care.light: Full sun, at least 6 hours a day

thymus_vulgaris.description: An aromatic sub-shrub with tiny leaves and an intense scent. Essential in Mediterranean cooking and great in a pot on the windowsill.
funFacts: In ancient Egypt it was used for embalming
Thymol from thyme has strong antibacterial properties
The more sun, the stronger the scent
It attracts bees – a great honey plant
A symbol of courage in the Middle Ages – knights carried it into battle
It can live for 5–10 years
diseases: Woody, sparse shoots = too little light
Yellow leaves = overwatering
Mould at the base = too damp, too cold
Brown tips = too little water after all
Bland taste = lack of sun
thymus_vulgaris.propagation: Semi-ripe cuttings in summer – cut a 10 cm shoot, strip the lower leaves and insert into sand mixed with peat.

ocimum_basilicum_thai.name: Thai basil
ocimum_basilicum_thai.description: A basil variety with darker stems and purple flower heads. It tastes of anise and liquorice – essential in Thai and Vietnamese cooking.
funFacts: Its taste differs from European basil – notes of anise and liquorice
The leaves are narrower and darker than those of ‘Genovese’
The stems and flowers have a purple tint
An ingredient of traditional dishes such as pho and pad krapow
It tolerates higher temperatures than European basil
After flowering the leaves lose their flavour – pinch off the flower heads
diseases: Flower heads = trim regularly so it doesn't bloom
Blackening leaves = too cold, below 15°C
Faded leaves = lack of nutrients
White mould = powdery mildew – ventilate better
Yellow lower leaves = natural or overwatering
ocimum_basilicum_thai.propagation: From seed or water cuttings – a 10 cm shoot in water roots within a week.

coriandrum_sativum.name: Coriander (Cilantro)

care.water: Every 2–3 days, keep the soil lightly moist
care.light: Bright, 4–5 hours of sun, but not scorching

coriandrum_sativum.description: An aromatic annual with a distinctive flavour that people either love or hate. Fresh, it's indispensable in Mexican, Indian and Thai cooking.
funFacts: Some people have a gene that makes coriander taste like soap
The leaves and seeds are two completely different flavours in cooking
It bolts very quickly in heat – and then turns bitter
The seeds are a classic warm spice
Rich in vitamins A, C and K
It grows best in spring and autumn and struggles in summer
diseases: Bolting quickly = too hot, it goes to seed
Yellow leaves = overwatering or exhausted soil
Aphids on the flower stalks
Mould with excess moisture
Weak growth = lack of light
coriandrum_sativum.propagation: Only from seed – it doesn't root from cuttings. Sow every 3–4 weeks for a continuous harvest.

origanum_vulgare.name: Oregano

care.water: Every 5–7 days, let it dry out between waterings

origanum_vulgare.description: A classic herb of Italian and Greek cooking. Its small, intensely aromatic leaves go with pizza, tomato sauces and barbecues.
funFacts: The name comes from Greek: ‘oros’ (mountain) and ‘ganos’ (joy) = ‘joy of the mountains’
In ancient Greece a symbol of love and happiness
Dried, it's more aromatic than fresh – one of the few herbs like that
A perennial – one plant can give you herbs for years
Bees love its purple flowers
Oregano oil has strong antibacterial properties
diseases: Woody stems = prune in spring to rejuvenate
Brown tips = too little water, even though it likes drying out
Mould = too damp, poor air flow
Pale colour = lack of sun
Powdery mildew in damp conditions
origanum_vulgare.propagation: Stem cuttings in spring, division or seed. Very easy.

citrus_limon.name: Lemon tree

care.water: Every 4–6 days in summer, less often in winter

citrus_limon.description: A lemon tree in a pot – the dream of many growers. It needs attention, but rewards you with fragrant flowers and real lemons.
funFacts: It can flower and fruit at the same time – flowers next to ripe fruit
The fruit takes 6–9 months to ripen
It needs a cool rest period in winter in order to flower
The buds are white outside and pinkish inside, and intensely fragrant
It needs special citrus fertiliser
In winter move it to an unheated room, e.g. a stairwell
diseases: Bud drop = stress, a change of spot or a draught
Yellow leaves with green veins = chlorosis, lack of iron
No fruit = too little sun or no cool rest
Mealybugs and scale insects – common on citrus
Sticky leaves = aphids
citrus_limon.propagation: Usually grafted onto rootstocks. From seed it grows slowly and doesn't always fruit. Cuttings are easier.

punica_granatum.name: Dwarf pomegranate

care.water: Every 4–5 days in summer, rarely in winter

punica_granatum.description: A dwarf pomegranate, ideal for a pot. Its red-orange trumpet-shaped flowers and miniature fruit are impressive despite its small size.
funFacts: The dwarf variety ‘Nana’ stays small but flowers profusely
The flowers are bright orange-red and bell-shaped
The fruit is small and mostly ornamental (bitter)
The leaves turn yellow and fall in autumn – it's deciduous
It needs a cool rest period in winter
A symbol of abundance in many Mediterranean cultures
diseases: Flower drop = too dry or too hot while flowering
No flowers = no winter rest
Yellow leaves in autumn = natural
Aphids on new shoots
Spider mites in dry air
punica_granatum.propagation: Semi-ripe cuttings in summer or rooted suckers from the roots.

coffea_arabica_dwarf.name: Dwarf Arabica coffee
coffea_arabica_dwarf.description: A real coffee plant in a pot. After 3–4 years it may bloom with fragrant white flowers and then produce red cherries with coffee beans inside.
funFacts: After 3–4 years of growing it flowers and fruits
Its white flowers smell like jasmine
Each red ‘cherry’ holds two coffee beans
The leaves contain a little caffeine – not for pets!
It comes from the mountain forests of Ethiopia
The most popular dwarf variety is ‘Nana’
diseases: Brown tips = low humidity
Yellow leaves = overwatering or exhausted soil
Scorched leaves = harsh sun
No flowers = too young or too dark
Blackening shoots = too cold
coffea_arabica_dwarf.propagation: From seed (fresh beans) or semi-ripe cuttings. Slow-growing.

stephanotis.name: Madagascar jasmine (Stephanotis)

care.water: Every 4–6 days in summer, less often in winter
care.light: Very bright, but no direct sun

stephanotis.description: A climber with intensely fragrant, waxy white flowers. A favourite for wedding bouquets thanks to its scent and looks.
funFacts: Also known as Madagascar jasmine or bridal wreath
Its flowers are used in wedding bouquets in many cultures
The scent is strongest in the evening – it attracts night-flying pollinators
It can live for decades in the right conditions
It needs a cool winter to flower in summer
A symbol of marital happiness
diseases: No flowers = no cool winter
Bud drop = draught or stress
Yellow leaves = overwatering
Mealybugs and scale insects
Sticky leaves = aphids
stephanotis.propagation: Semi-ripe cuttings in spring – rooting is difficult and needs bottom heat.

schlumbergera.name: Christmas cactus (Schlumbergera)
schlumbergera.description: Despite the name “cactus”, it's a plant of tropical forests, not the desert. It flowers profusely in winter – hence the name “Christmas cactus”.
funFacts: In the wild it grows on trees as an epiphyte
Flowering depends on day length – shorter days trigger buds
It can live 30–50 years
Easy to propagate – break off a segment, leave it for a day, plant it
Varieties in pink, red, white, orange and purple
Safe for pets
diseases: Bud drop = a change of spot or sudden temperature swings
No flowers = no cool autumn with short days
Limp segments = overwatering and rotting roots
Orange segments = too much sun
Cracked segments = excessive watering
schlumbergera.propagation: The easiest – break off 2–3 segments, leave them for a day, plant in a light mix. Roots form within 2 weeks.

spathiphyllum_picasso.name: Peace lily ‘Picasso’
spathiphyllum_picasso.description: A variegated peace lily – its leaves are covered with white patches and stripes. All the advantages of the ordinary peace lily plus a dramatic look.
funFacts: Every leaf has a unique white pattern – like a Picasso painting
It needs more light than the ordinary form to keep its patterns
Like the ordinary one, it blooms with white “sails”
A great water indicator – it droops when it needs a drink
It purifies the air – removes formaldehyde and benzene
Less vigorous than the classic – the patterns cost energy
diseases: Fading patterns = too little light
Brown tips = hard water or low humidity
Drooping leaves = lack of water (they lift after watering)
Scorched leaves = direct sun
No flowers = too young or too dark
spathiphyllum_picasso.propagation: Only by dividing the clump when repotting.

anthurium_clarinervium.name: Velvet cardboard anthurium (A. clarinervium)
anthurium_clarinervium.description: A foliage anthurium rather than a flowering one – heart-shaped leaves with dramatic silver veins like lace. A fashionable species among collectors.
funFacts: The leaves are velvety to the touch
Young leaves are light brown and mature to dark green
The silver veins are more distinct in shade than in sun
A pricey species – the price rises with size
In the wild it grows in limestone forests – it prefers a mineral substrate
Its flowers are modest – it's grown for its leaves
diseases: Brown tips = hard water or low humidity
Fading veins = too much sun
Yellow leaves = overwatering
Black spots = fungus from excess moisture
Slow growth is normal – it's a slow-growing species
anthurium_clarinervium.propagation: Division or root cuttings. Difficult – not for beginners.

tradescantia_nanouk.name: Tradescantia ‘Nanouk’

care.water: Every 5–7 days, once the top of the soil is dry
care.light: Bright, a few hours of sun to keep the colour

tradescantia_nanouk.description: A trendy tradescantia with striped leaves in pink, green and cream. Very easy, fast-growing and ideal for hanging pots.
funFacts: Bred in the Netherlands in 2012
The more light, the more intense the pink stripes
The leaves are fleshy and slightly fuzzy
It breaks easily when repotting – handle it gently
It blooms with small pink flowers
The sap can irritate skin and may be toxic to pets
diseases: Fading pink stripes = too little light
Long, bare stems = too little light
Yellow lower leaves = natural or overwatering
Brown tips = air too dry
Limp leaves = lack of water
tradescantia_nanouk.propagation: The easiest – cut a 10 cm stem, put it in water or soil, it roots within a week.

alocasia_polly.name: Alocasia ‘Polly’ (African mask)
alocasia_polly.description: A small but striking alocasia with dark, glossy leaves and white veins. Known for its dramatic looks and demanding nature.
funFacts: A cross between A. longiloba and A. sanderiana
Its leaves are almost black with white veins
Each leaf lasts a few months, then turns yellow and drops
It forms a corm – after stress it can die back and regrow from it
It likes stable conditions – every change is stressful
In winter it may go dormant and lose all its leaves
diseases: Yellow, dropping leaves = overwatering or the natural cycle
Brown tips = low humidity
Faded veins = too little light
Spider mites in dry air
Scorched leaves = harsh sun
alocasia_polly.propagation: Dividing the corm or offsets from the corm. Difficult, for experienced growers.

ficus_audrey.name: Ficus ‘Audrey’ (Banyan fig)

care.water: Every 7–10 days, once the top of the soil is dry

ficus_audrey.description: A fashionable alternative to the fiddle-leaf fig – velvety, oval leaves with distinct pale veins. Less fussy than the fiddle-leaf, but just as decorative.
funFacts: In India it's a sacred tree – the banyan fig
The leaves are slightly velvety to the touch
Less demanding than the fiddle-leaf fig, with a similar look
It can grow into a giant tree – up to 30 m in the wild
It produces aerial roots
The milky sap can irritate skin
diseases: Dropping leaves = overwatering or stress from changes
Brown edges = low humidity
Lower leaves yellowing and dropping = natural or overwatering
Limp leaves = lack of water
Scale insects and mealybugs
ficus_audrey.propagation: Semi-ripe cuttings – cut a 15 cm shoot and root it in water or straight into soil under plastic.

sansevieria_cylindrica.name: Cylindrical snake plant

care.water: Every 14–21 days, the soil must be dry
care.light: Tolerates everything – from sun to partial shade

sansevieria_cylindrica.description: A snake plant with cylindrical, stiff leaves that look like spears. Sellers often braid them. Extremely tough.
funFacts: Its leaves are round in cross-section, not flat like the ordinary one
Often sold “braided” – with the leaves woven together
It stores water in its leaves like a succulent
It produces oxygen at night – great for the bedroom
One of the most durable houseplants
It can live for decades with little care
diseases: Wrinkled leaves = lack of water (rare)
Limp, brown leaves = overwatering and rot
Black spots at the base = excess moisture
Slow growth = normal
No new shoots = too little light
sansevieria_cylindrica.propagation: From offsets – cut a young shoot with a piece of root. Leaf cuttings also root, but slowly.

asparagus_setaceus.name: Asparagus fern
asparagus_setaceus.description: Not a true fern, although it looks like one – delicate, lacy sprays that create a green mist. A favourite filler in flower bouquets.
funFacts: Despite looking like a fern, it's a flowering plant of the asparagus family
Related to the edible vegetable asparagus
Red berries appear after inconspicuous white flowers
Used in bouquets as background greenery
The stems are very delicate – easily damaged
There are small thorns on the stems – take care when handling
diseases: Yellowing stems = overwatering or too cold
Brown tips = low humidity
Bare centre = too little light
Spider mites in dry air
Small aphids on new shoots
asparagus_setaceus.propagation: Divide the clump when repotting or grow from seed (slow).

philodendron_brasil.name: Philodendron ‘Brasil’
philodendron_brasil.description: A variegated heartleaf philodendron – its leaves have lime-green and creamy-yellow stripes. Just as easy as the ordinary form, twice as pretty.
funFacts: Named after the colours of the Brazilian flag – green and yellow
Every leaf is different – the variegation is random
Sometimes it produces an all-green or all-yellow leaf
The brighter the light (without harsh sun), the more yellow
Very easy to propagate – like pothos
It can grow on a support (the leaves get bigger) or trail
diseases: Less variegation = too little light
All-yellow leaves lacking green have too little chlorophyll and may die
Yellowing leaves = overwatering
Brown tips = low humidity
Slow growth in winter
philodendron_brasil.propagation: Stem cuttings – like an ordinary philodendron. Choose a stem with lots of variegation.

begonia_maculata_alba.name: Angel wing begonia (B. maculata ‘Alba’)

care.water: Every 4–6 days, once the top of the soil is dry

begonia_maculata_alba.description: A spectacular begonia with polka-dot leaves – dark green with white dots and red undersides. It blooms with cascades of white or pink flowers.
funFacts: It inspired polka-dot designs
The underside of the leaf is dark red – a contrast with the green top
It forms cascades of white flowers that hang like coral
Its stems are bamboo-like – hence the name “angel wing begonia”
Easy to propagate from cuttings
In the wild it grows in Brazil's forests, in damp undergrowth
diseases: Fading dots = too much light
No flowers = too dark or lack of nutrients
Powdery mildew – a common begonia disease
Yellow leaves = overwatering
Dropping leaves = a sudden change in conditions
begonia_maculata_alba.propagation: Stem cuttings with 1 node – they root in water within 2 weeks.

musa_dwarf.name: Dwarf banana
musa_dwarf.description: A dwarf banana you can grow at home. After 2–3 years it may produce real bananas – small, but edible.
funFacts: A banana isn't a tree but a perennial herb – the “trunk” is rolled-up leaves
After fruiting the plant dies, but leaves offsets
The dwarf variety ‘Super Dwarf Cavendish’ reaches 1.5 m at most
Its leaves can be a metre long
It needs lots of water and light
It grows fast – in season it can put out a new leaf every week
diseases: Split leaves = natural, bananas just do that
Brown tips = low humidity
Yellow leaves = overwatering or lack of nutrients
No flowers = too young or too cold
Spider mites in dry air
musa_dwarf.propagation: From suckers growing from the rhizome. Very hard from seed – most varieties are sterile.

rosmarinus.name: Rosemary

care.water: Every 5–7 days, the soil must dry out between waterings
care.light: Full sun, at least 6 hours a day

rosmarinus.description: A classic herb of Mediterranean cooking. Its aromatic, needle-like leaves smell of pine and citrus. It needs sun and good drainage.
funFacts: Botanically it belongs to the sage genus (since 2017)
A symbol of remembrance in many cultures
It can live for decades and turn woody
It blooms with blue flowers that bees love
Rosemary oil has anti-inflammatory properties
In ancient Rome it was planted near houses for luck
diseases: Woody with few green needles = prune in spring
Mould at the base = too damp, poor drainage
Pale needles = lack of iron
Powdery mildew in hot, humid air
Slow growth in winter – normal
rosmarinus.propagation: Semi-ripe cuttings in summer – cut a 10 cm shoot, strip the lower needles and insert into sand.

stromanthe_triostar.name: Stromanthe ‘Triostar’
stromanthe_triostar.description: A spectacular member of the Marantaceae family – its leaves are green, cream and pink, some even striped. In the evening it folds its leaves up like praying hands.
funFacts: The underside of the leaf is bright pink
In the evening it raises its leaves – a “prayer plant”
Every leaf has a unique variegation pattern
Safe for pets
It needs soft water – left to stand, or rainwater
Sensitive to change – it dislikes being moved
diseases: Brown tips = hard water or low humidity
Scorched white parts = light too bright
Curled leaves = lack of water or a draught
Fading pink = too little light
Spider mites in dry air
stromanthe_triostar.propagation: Only by dividing the clump when repotting – stem cuttings don't root.

kalanchoe_thyrsiflora.name: Paddle plant (Flapjacks)

care.water: Every 10–14 days, the soil must dry out
care.light: Full sun – the more, the redder the edges

kalanchoe_thyrsiflora.description: A succulent with flat, round leaves that look like a stack of pancakes. The leaf edges turn red in the sun.
funFacts: Also called “paddle plant” or “flapjacks”
Its leaves are round and flat, as if stacked in a column
The more sun, the more intense the red edges
After many years it blooms with yellow flowers and then dies – but leaves offsets
The powdery coating on the leaves is natural protection
Toxic to cats and dogs – be careful!
diseases: Stretching and losing shape = too little light
Yellowing leaves = overwatering
No red = too little sun
Wrinkled leaves = lack of water (rare)
Powdery mildew in air that's too humid
kalanchoe_thyrsiflora.propagation: From a leaf – break off a lower leaf, let it dry for 2 days and lay it on soil. Or from offsets.
